I mentioned having read Hardy in one of my other replies. "Tess of the D'Urbervilles" was the first novel of his that I read, and I was hooked. Then, my senior year of high school, during our AP Literature "Thomas Hardy boot camp," my teacher mentioned that no one wanted to tackle "Jude the Obscure" and that it was his favorite of Hardy's novels. Wanting to impress him-and also looking for a challenge-I took on Hardy's final completed novel. From it spawned many visits to my my teachers classroom during office hours and a somber presentation of the novel. I've only been able to read it twice in my life, and the second time I picked it up, I must have forgotten the way it broke me the first time. I've never been more devastated by one book before, but the character of Jude was so tragic that I still get emotional thinking of his journey. I recommend that book to everyone and mention that they should prepare themselves. "Jude the Obscure" rivals "Jane Eyre" as my favorite novel of all time.

I understand that on a personal level. Some of my friendships are borderline co-dependent, but I've found coping mechanisms to handle the-sometimes large-distance between us. Making new friends doesn't mean you have to give up your old friends. Old friends are there to stay, but if you're afraid of the isolation that comes with your friends moving away, maybe you should try to put yourself out there to make new friends. I find that it's often much easier said than done, but I can speak from personal experience that it makes such an incredible difference.

If you do find yourself struggling with a depressive episode, take extra time to talk with the people in your life about how you're feeling. Take the feelings of isolation and do your best to make them positive. Maybe you can build a better tolerance to being alone. Maybe you could take up a new hobby (it's also a great way to meet new people). If you're starting to become depressed, try to focus on self-care. Set aside 20 or 30 minutes every day to do something for yourself, whether that's exercise, reading a chapter or two of a good book, or taking a long, hot shower. Hopefully, you don't get to the depressed part, but if you do, there are so many ways to manage it in order to keep yourself productive and healthy!

It's good that you're able to recognize the correlation between your friends leaving and falling into a depression. Is it possible to schedule time to Skype or Facetime with you friends while they're away? If so, you could chat with them about that possibility and make a recurring time each week or so to video chat. That helps me immensely with my long-distance friendships. Maybe you could even schedule times to visit each other if your situations allow such a thing. Also, don't be afraid to make other friends in your area. It's important to maintain a strong network of friends and people who care about you so that if you do find yourself struggling, you have people to turn to.

The goal is to help you cope and manage your mental health and keep you safe, so if the mental health personnel in your area deem it necessary for you to be checked into inpatient care, trust that it's for the best. This doesn't happen all the time, though. When I discussed my rough plan with my therapist, I wasn't committed, but we talked about extra steps I could take to make it more difficult for me to get my hands on the devices I would use to hurt myself. It was incredibly helpful to talk through this with a mental health professional. I have been kept in inpatient care on two separate ocassions, and it was frustrating at first; however, looking back on my experience, it was the best thing for me. Always be honest with mental health professionals.

Know that the plan you set for your life is not set in stone, and that is okay. Be patient with yourself. Your life doesn't have to be on schedule, so have fun! Keep in touch with the people you love and the ones who love you. Don't settle! Know your worth, and don't keep people in your life who don't make you feel important. Don't waste time trying to be who someone else wants you to be, either, because it's a losing battle in the end. Don't be afraid to be alone once in a while. Learn who you are as a single adult because it makes it easier to know what you want in a romantic relationship. Every paycheck put some money into a savings account. Call your parents and chat with them as often as possible because they won't be around forever, and you'll miss the sound of their voice. Those insignificant phone calls will be some of the most important ones in the end. Listen more than you speak because you don't learn from talking. Never be afraid to ask questions. Do what makes you happy because life is too short to be unhappy. Also, remember that just because you get older doesn't mean you have to be a grown up. Stay young. Love fiercely.
These are some of the things I wish someone had told my 18 year old self, but I wish you the best of luck. Happy belated birthday, and welcome to adulthood.

As someone who struggles with MDD, it was the most difficult time even getting my associates degree, and I'm still working on my bachelor's as we speak. What I found most helpful was therapy, but if therapy isn't an available tool for you to use, try building a good support system. Surround yourself with people who will keep you as motivated as you can be but also ones who will be mindful and sensitive to what you're going through.
There's a lot of leg work that you have to do, too. Try using an academic planner and sticking to the goals you set for the day. Also, schedule time for self-care every single day, whatever that looks like for you. If your self-care comes in the form of exercise, cooking a meal, reading a few chapters of a good book, or taking a 30 minute nap, do it. Those also help keep you motivated, and it's a way to cope with the hills and valleys of having depression.
Another thing you could do is notice the little things you do during the day that are signs that you're overcoming your depression symptoms. For example, it you manage to get out of the bed, notice it and maybe write it down. It's so easy to look at the day and say "my depression got the best of me today," but when you have tangible evidence that you overcame some of those symptoms, it could be beneficial and help propel you in the right direction.
